title: Do You Really Need Multivitamins, or Are Managu and Githeri Enough?
markdown_body:
You have probably stood in a chemist in Nairobi, Mombasa, or Kisumu and stared at a wall of multivitamin bottles. Glowing skin. Boundless energy. A better you, for the price of a lunch. Then you go home to githeri and wonder if the bottle is just expensive urine.

Most of the time, the plate wins. Managu, terere, kunde, beans, eggs, and a spoon of omena already carry the vitamins and minerals a mixed diet is supposed to give you. The NHS says the same thing in fewer words: eat a varied diet and you cover the basics. A capsule is for the gap, not for replacing lunch.

![A bowl of vegetables, chickpeas, and avocado](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1512621776951-a57141f2eefd?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

### The vitamins your body does not keep

Before you swallow a high dose, it helps to know what your body actually holds onto.

Vitamin C and the B vitamins are the ones you use and lose. You need them again tomorrow, and anything extra leaves in your urine. This is also why the way you cook matters. Boil sukuma wiki or cabbage for ages and the goodness ends up in the pot water. Steam it, or fry it quickly, and more of it stays on the plate.

Vitamins A, D, E, and K are different. They sit in your liver and body fat, waiting. You find them in oily fish, eggs, liver, and milk. Because they stay, a huge dose every day can pile up. That is when a "more is better" bottle stops being harmless.

### What those tiny units on the label mean

The label is doing a lot of work in very small letters.

1. **mg** is a milligram, a thousandth of a gram.
2. **mcg** or **μg** is a microgram, a millionth of a gram. One thousand micrograms make one milligram.
3. **IU** means international units. You will see it on vitamins A, D, and E.

A pill will not do the job of a balanced plate. It earns its place in pregnancy, in early childhood, on a strict vegan diet that needs vitamin B12, or when a test has already shown you are low. Everything else is optional. Your sukuma is not.
meta_title: Do You Really Need Multivitamins or Is a Kenyan Diet Enough?
meta_description: Managu, githeri, and omena already cover more than most multivitamin labels admit. Here is when a tablet still earns its place.

title: The Equatorial Paradox: Why Do So Many Kenyans Have Low Vitamin D?
markdown_body:
Kenya sits on the equator. The sun is not the problem. So why do labs in Nairobi and Eldoret keep handing people vitamin D results that come back low?

It feels backwards. We have sunshine from January to December, and still the "sunshine vitamin" runs short. Vitamin D is what helps your body use calcium and phosphate, which is a long way of saying it looks after your bones, teeth, muscles, and the part of you that fights a cold.

![Sunrise over a green hillside](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1470252649378-9c29740c9fa8?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

### The sun is there. Your skin is not in it.

Three ordinary things get in the way.

You leave the house at 6:30, sit under office lights, and get home after 6. The hours when the sun would actually make vitamin D happen while you are behind glass. A matatu window does not count.

Dark and brown skin has more melanin. That is a gift in this climate. It also slows the rate at which skin turns sunlight into vitamin D, so the same twenty minutes does less for you than it would for someone with very light skin.

And if you keep most of your skin covered, for faith, for comfort, or simply because the sun is fierce, there is less surface left to do the job.

### How much is enough, and how much is too much

If you rarely get proper sun, 10 micrograms a day is the usual maintenance dose. That is 400 IU. It is the figure the NHS gives adults and children over one who are not getting much daylight, and it fits a Nairobi routine better than we like to admit.

Food helps, it just rarely closes the gap on its own. Oily fish, omena, egg yolks, red meat, liver, and fortified spreads or cereals are the ones worth putting on the weekly menu.

Do not freelance a huge dose. Unless a doctor has seen your blood test and given you a short loading course, stay under 100 micrograms a day, which is 4,000 IU. Past that, calcium can build up in the blood. Bones suffer, and so can the kidneys and the heart.
meta_title: Why So Many Kenyans Have Low Vitamin D Despite Year-Round Sun
meta_description: Kenya has sun all year, yet plenty of us still run low on vitamin D. Office hours, melanin, and covered skin are the usual reasons.

title: Expecting a Baby? The Essential Guide to Pregnancy Supplements (And What to Avoid!)
markdown_body:
The test turns positive, or you are trying, and suddenly every auntie has a bottle for you. Some of that advice is gold. Some of it is the cod liver oil you were given as a child, and that one needs to stay in the cupboard.

A colourful plate still feeds the pregnancy. A few nutrients are hard to get reliably from food alone, and those are the ones worth being boring about.

![A newborn's feet on a white blanket](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1555252333-9f8e92e65df9?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

### Folic acid, before the bump even shows

Folic acid is the one to start early. It cuts the risk of problems in the baby's brain and spine, including spina bifida, and it is also tied to a lower risk of cleft lip and some heart conditions.

Take 400 micrograms every day. Ideally you start three months before you conceive and you keep going through the first 12 weeks. If you waited until the clinic visit, start the day you know. Late is still better than never.

Some people need 5 milligrams, and that dose comes from a doctor, not from the chemist shelf. Ask if you have diabetes, sickle cell, or thalassaemia, if you take medicine for HIV or epilepsy, or if neural tube problems run in the family. That is the point where the NHS stops saying "just take the standard tablet" and says get a prescription.

### Vitamin D, iron, and the bottle to leave alone

Vitamin D, 10 micrograms (400 IU) a day, helps the baby's bones and teeth. Darker skin and indoor days mean many of us are not making enough from the sun, so taking it through the pregnancy is a quiet, useful habit.

Iron is the other one clinics watch closely. About a third of pregnant women in Kenya are anaemic. Your haemoglobin gets checked at the first antenatal visit and again around 28 weeks. If it is low, or you are simply on the usual iron and folic acid they give in pregnancy, that daily iron is what keeps you from dragging yourself through the day.

Now the warning, because this one surprises people. Cod liver oil was a tonic in a lot of Kenyan childhoods. In pregnancy, leave it. The same goes for any multivitamin that contains vitamin A as retinol, and for liver on the plate. Too much preformed vitamin A can harm the baby. Pick a prenatal, or plain folic acid plus vitamin D. Do not grab the adult multivitamin that was fine before you conceived.
meta_title: Essential Pregnancy Supplements Guide: Folic Acid, Iron & Vitamin D
meta_description: What to take when you are pregnant or trying, from folic acid and iron to vitamin D, and why cod liver oil can wait.

title: Liquid Drops, Gummies, or Formula? Smart Vitamin Rules for Babies & Under-5s
markdown_body:
The weaning plate starts so well. Mashed matoke, pumpkin, a little porridge. Then the fussy season arrives and you are negotiating three spoons like it is a peace talk. Of course you wonder if they are getting enough.

Small children grow fast, and food alone does not always cover vitamins A, C, and D between six months and five years. A daily drop is the usual advice, including from the NHS. The trick is knowing which child needs it, and which child is already getting it in their milk.

![Mango, kiwi, grapes, and other fresh fruit](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1619566636858-adf3ef46400b?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

### What A, C, and D are actually doing

Vitamin A looks after vision in dim light, the skin, and the lining that helps a child fight infection. In Kenya this one matters. More than half of children under five are low in it. Mangoes, carrots, viazi vitamu, spinach, and milk are the foods that help.

Vitamin C keeps immune cells happy and helps a small body pull iron out of plant food. Oranges, tomatoes, peppers, and pawpaw do this job well.

Vitamin D is the bone builder. Skip it for long enough in a growing child and you are in rickets territory.

### Breast milk, formula, and the 500 ml line

Not every baby needs the same bottle from day one.

A breastfed baby needs a vitamin D drop from birth, about 8.5 to 10 micrograms a day, even if you are taking vitamin D yourself. Your milk is wonderful. It is just not a reliable vitamin D delivery service.

A formula-fed baby drinking 500 ml or more a day should not get an extra vitamin D drop. The formula is already fortified with A, C, and D. Adding a drop on top is how you overshoot.

From age one to four, go back to a daily supplement with 10 micrograms of vitamin D, plus A and C.

### One bottle. Not two.

This is the rule that saves you a frightened evening. Do not give two supplements on the same day. Drops plus cod liver oil, or drops plus gummies, is how a toddler gets too much A and D. Cod liver oil is already rich in both. Young livers do not need a double serving. Pick one product, read the label, and leave the second one in the cupboard.
meta_title: Vitamins for Babies & Children Under 5: Liquid Drops & Dosage Rules
meta_description: A simple guide for parents on vitamin drops, the formula rule, and why two bottles at once is too much for a small child.

title: Strong Bones After 65: How to Protect Your Mobility and Prevent Fractures
markdown_body:
Ask anyone looking after a parent over 65 and the fear is the same. Not a dramatic illness. A small slip, a swollen wrist, and suddenly the person who walked to the kiosk needs help to the bathroom.

Bone thins as we age. After menopause it thins faster, because oestrogen was doing quiet protective work. If calcium runs low, the body takes it from the skeleton. The bone gets porous. Osteoporosis is just the medical name for a hip that breaks too easily.

![An older woman outdoors with her daughter](https://images.pexels.com/photos/3768131/pexels-photo-3768131.jpeg?auto=compress&cs=tinysrgb&w=1600)

### Calcium without vitamin D is a wasted effort

You can drink all the maziwa mala you like. Without vitamin D, the gut does not absorb the calcium properly. The two have to travel together.

Aim for at least 700 mg of calcium a day, and closer to 1,200 mg after menopause. The NHS sits in that same range for people over 65. You can get there with mala, yoghurt, milk, fortified soy, beans, nuts, and sukuma wiki. The local secret is fish you eat bones and all. Omena, sardines, and anchovies are some of the best bone food on earth, and they are already in the market.

Older skin makes less vitamin D from the sun, and a lot of parents spend the bright hours indoors. A daily vitamin D3 supplement, about 10 micrograms (400 to 800 IU), is what lets the calcium in the meal actually reach the bone.

If food is not enough and you add a calcium tablet, the type matters. Calcium carbonate is the concentrated one, and it needs a meal so stomach acid can work on it. Calcium citrate is gentler and does not mind an empty stomach.

### The bones still need a reason to stay

A tablet is half the job. Bone is living tissue. It stays dense when you load it. Brisk walking, gardening, a bit of dancing, light strength work: about 150 minutes of that kind of movement a week, plus something that challenges balance so falls happen less often. Smoking and a heavy drinking habit undo a lot of this. Cutting back is not a lecture. It is bone you get to keep.
meta_title: Strong Bones Over 65: Calcium, Vitamin D & Osteoporosis Prevention
meta_description: How to keep bones steady after 65 with calcium, vitamin D, omena, and a bit of walking. Joints included.

title: Always Tired and Catching Every Cold? 3 Hidden Deficiencies to Check
markdown_body:
There is a kind of tired that sleep does not fix. You blame the traffic, the weather, the week. Then the cold you caught in the matatu is still sitting on your chest two weeks later, and "I am just busy" stops being a good enough story.

In Kenya, that pattern often comes back to three quiet shortages: iron, zinc, and vitamin B12.

![A pile of fresh oranges](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1611080626919-7cf5a9dbab5b?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80)

### Iron, and the tea you should move

Iron builds haemoglobin, the part of blood that carries oxygen to your brain and your legs. Run low, and the tiredness is not ordinary. You look pale. Stairs make you breathless. Your heart races for no good reason. Women with heavy periods know this one too well.

Liver, beef, beans, lentils, and dark greens are the food fix. If the iron is coming from plants, or from a tablet, pair it with vitamin C. Orange juice, a squeeze of lemon, or a vitamin C tablet helps the body take it in. And shift the chai. Tea and coffee with the meal block iron. Have them later, not on top of the greens.

### Zinc, the reason a cold will not leave

A lot of Kenyan children, up to about 70 percent in survey data, are not getting enough zinc, and plenty of adults are in the same boat. Zinc is what wakes up the immune cells, closes a cut, and keeps food tasting like food.

The signs are unglamorous. Colds that linger, cuts that take forever, thinning hair, diarrhoea that keeps coming back. Pumpkin seeds, meat, shellfish, milk, and chickpeas help. In cold season a modest tablet, 10 to 15 mg, is plenty. Stay under 25 mg a day if you are taking it for months. Past that, the NHS warns, zinc starts blocking copper and can leave you anaemic. More is not a stronger immune system.

### Vitamin B12, when the tiredness comes with tingling

B12 makes red blood cells and looks after the nerves. About 35 percent of Kenyan women of childbearing age, and around 70 percent of school-age children, sit at low or borderline levels, mostly because animal food is not on the plate often enough.

Brain fog, a memory that keeps slipping, exhaustion that does not match your sleep, and pins and needles in the hands or feet are the clues. B12 lives in meat, fish, milk, and eggs. If you eat mostly plants, or you are on metformin for diabetes, a daily B12 or a B complex is not a luxury. It is the missing piece.
meta_title: Always Tired & Getting Sick? Check Iron, Zinc & Vitamin B12 Levels
meta_description: If you are always tired or catching every cold, iron, zinc, and vitamin B12 are the three gaps worth checking.
